---
title: "How Pretraining Works"
subtitle: "The objective, the loss, the optimization loop, and what they do and do not teach the model"
---

*Prerequisites: basic probability (a product of probabilities; a
logarithm) and the idea of a weighted sum. `learn/neural-networks.qmd`
works through loss, gradient, backpropagation, and the optimizer step on
one unit; this page uses those words with one-clause reminders and links
there for the derivation.*

## 1. The objective

An autoregressive language model predicts each token from the tokens that
came before it. That single sentence is the whole training objective, and
the rest of this page unpacks it.

Write a training sequence of $T$ tokens as $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_T$. The
probability the model assigns to the entire sequence is built from
one-step predictions, one per position:

$$
p(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_T) = \prod_{t=1}^{T} p(x_t \mid x_{<t})
$$

Read the right-hand side as: the probability of the first token, times
the probability of the second token given the first, times the
probability of the third given the first two, and so on. The notation
$x_{<t}$ means "all the tokens before position $t$", and $\prod$ means
"multiply these together". Nothing is being assumed about the text; any
joint probability over a sequence can be written as such a chain of
conditionals, and language modeling has long been framed as estimating
exactly this product of next-symbol conditionals. [S-40] [S-41] What the
model provides is each factor: at every position, a probability
distribution over the vocabulary for the next token, given the tokens so
far.

The targets come from the text itself. `learn/how-created.qmd` shows the
shift-by-one construction: at each position that has a following token,
that following token is the target. Equivalently, the representation the
network computes at input position $t$ is used to predict $x_{t+1}$. One
bookkeeping point reconciles this with the product above. The very first
factor, $p(x_1)$, conditions on nothing, so in practice a model predicts
the first token from a conventional start-of-sequence marker or from
preceding context. For the five-token sentence used on this and the
earlier page, the course conditions on the first displayed token and
shows the four following-token targets. No labels are written by anyone;
a body of text supplies one target per position with a successor.

## 2. Training evaluates many positions at once

Generation is sequential by nature. The model predicts a distribution
for the next token, one token is selected, it is appended to the
sequence, and the next prediction depends on the token that was actually
chosen. Nothing about step $t+1$ can begin until step $t$ has produced its
token.

Training is different, and the difference is what makes transformers
practical to train. A training sequence is complete before training
touches it: $x_1$ through $x_T$ are all known. The network can therefore
compute its prediction at every position in a single forward pass,
provided the prediction at position $t$ is prevented from using the
tokens after $t$. That is exactly what causal masking does, as
`learn/transformers-attention.qmd` §4 describes: the scores for future
positions are removed before softmax, so the representation at position
$t$ depends only on positions $1$ to $t$. [S-22] With the mask in place,
the prediction at position 1, the prediction at position 2, and every
other prediction are computed from the same forward pass, and their
losses are computed together. A recurrent network cannot do this, because
its computation at each position waits for the previous position to
finish; the original Transformer paper gives removing that sequential
dependency as a central motivation. [S-16]

So the model is trained in parallel across positions and used
sequentially across positions. The two computations share the same
parameters and the same masking rule, and they differ in what is known
in advance.

## 3. From logits to loss

At each position the transformer's final layer produces one raw score
per vocabulary entry; machine-learning literature calls these scores
logits. Softmax maps them into a probability distribution over the
vocabulary, exactly as `learn/softmax-sampling.qmd` works through. [S-05]
[S-30] The observed next token, the target, picks out one entry of that
distribution. Write $p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t})$ for the probability the
model, with its current parameters $\theta$, assigns to the token that
actually came next. The loss at that position is

$$
L_t = -\log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t})
$$

the negative logarithm of the probability given to the correct token. This
is the **negative log-likelihood**, and for a distribution produced by
softmax it is the same quantity as the cross-entropy loss that
`learn/neural-networks.qmd` uses for its single unit, now with a
vocabulary-sized set of categories instead of two. A few values show its
shape: if the model gave the correct token probability 1, the loss would
be 0; probability 0.5 gives a loss of about 0.69; probability 0.05 gives
about 3.0. The loss falls as the probability assigned to the observed
token rises, and it rises without bound as that probability approaches
zero. Lowering the loss therefore means, and can only mean, raising the
probability the model assigns to what actually came next.

For a sequence, the per-position losses are added up (or averaged over
the target positions); for a batch of sequences, over all their target
positions. Because $\log$ turns a product into a sum, the summed loss is
exactly $-\log$ of the sequence probability in §1:

$$
\sum_{t} L_t = -\log \prod_{t} p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t})
$$

Minimizing the summed negative log-likelihood is therefore the same thing
as maximizing the probability the model assigns to the observed training
tokens, which makes this **maximum-likelihood training**. [S-05] [S-41]
It is maximum-likelihood training, but it is not a conventional
econometric exercise aimed at identifying interpretable structural
parameters or reporting classical standard errors: the parameters are
the millions or billions of numbers inside a network, none of which is
meant to be read as a coefficient, and the goal is predictive fit. That
is a statement about what this training is for, not a claim that
uncertainty about a model's outputs is impossible to measure. [S-06]

## 4. The optimization loop

Pretraining is the loop that `learn/neural-networks.qmd` runs once on a
single unit, run an enormous number of times on the whole network:

1. sample a **mini-batch**, a small set of token sequences drawn from the
   training text;
2. run a forward pass on each sequence, producing a distribution over the
   next token at every position;
3. compute the loss $L_t$ at every target position;
4. combine those into one batch loss, by summing or averaging;
5. run **backpropagation**, which computes the gradient of the batch loss
   with respect to every trainable parameter, that is, how the loss would
   change with a small change in each parameter, at the current values;
6. let the **optimizer** use those gradients to update the parameters;
7. repeat with the next mini-batch.

Two points from the single-unit lesson carry over unchanged. First,
backpropagation computes gradients and does nothing else; a separate
optimizer step performs the update. [S-14] Second, the update is a small
step, taken many times. Two different gradients are worth keeping apart
here. Backpropagation computes the gradient of the current mini-batch's
loss exactly, up to ordinary numerical precision. But the mini-batch is
only a sample of the training data, so that mini-batch gradient is a
noisy estimate of the gradient of the full-data objective, and it varies
from batch to batch; this is why the procedure is called stochastic
optimization. The original Transformer was trained with Adam, a rule that
adapts the step size for each parameter using running averages of past
gradients. [S-42] The details of optimizer design are beyond this page.

What are the trainable parameters? Everything in the network that
training is allowed to change: the token embedding table; the query, key,
value, and output projection matrices in every attention layer; the
weights and biases of every feed-forward sublayer; the scaling parameters
of the normalization layers, where the architecture has them; and the
final projection that turns the last representation into logits over the
vocabulary. [S-29] [S-30] [S-36] [S-38] Backpropagation computes the
gradients for the trainable parameters at step 5, and the optimizer uses
those gradients to determine their updates at step 6.

## 5. A small numerical example

Take the sentence from `learn/how-created.qmd`, "The bridge was closed.",
tokenized illustratively as `The`, ` bridge`, ` was`, ` closed`, `.`. The
four positions with a following token give four targets. Suppose a model
A assigns the probabilities in the third column to the correct next
token at each position, and a better-trained model B assigns those in the
fifth column. The numbers are invented; the arithmetic is not.

<!-- check:likelihood -->

| Position | Target | $p_A$ | $-\log p_A$ | $p_B$ | $-\log p_B$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | ` bridge` | 0.60 | 0.511 | 0.80 | 0.223 |
| 2 | ` was` | 0.22 | 1.514 | 0.50 | 0.693 |
| 3 | ` closed` | 0.05 | 2.996 | 0.30 | 1.204 |
| 4 | `.` | 0.40 | 0.916 | 0.70 | 0.357 |
| Sum | | | 5.937 | | 2.477 |
| Mean | | | 1.484 | | 0.619 |

Model B assigns more probability to every correct token, so every
per-position loss is smaller, and its mean loss over the four targets is
0.619 against model A's 1.484. The sums say the same thing in the language
of §1: the conditional probability model A assigns to this four-target
continuation, given the initial displayed token, is the product
$0.60 \times 0.22 \times 0.05 \times 0.40 =
0.00264$, and $-\log 0.00264 = 5.937$, the summed loss; for model B the
product is $0.084$ and its negative log is $2.477$. Among the four
positions, ` closed` under model A, at probability 0.05, contributes the
largest token-level loss. Every number in the table is recomputed by
`scripts/check_training_example.py`.

## 6. What pretraining learns

The objective rewards one thing: assigning higher probability to the
observed next token. It provides no verified database of facts, no
hand-written rules of grammar, no human-defined list of meanings, and no
separate objective that checks whether a statement is true. During
pretraining, all parameter updates are driven by this prediction
objective. Capabilities that emerge from pretraining therefore emerge
under optimization of next-token prediction, even though the objective
does not explicitly label syntax, semantics, factual knowledge, or
reasoning as separate tasks.

Prediction on that scale turns out to require a great deal. To predict
the next token well, a network benefits from internal representations
that capture syntax, word meaning, factual associations that recur in
the data, conventions of discourse, and patterns of reasoning as
expressed in text, among many other regularities present in it. An early
neural language model already explained its generalization this way:
words used in similar contexts come to have similar learned vectors, so
that a sequence never seen in training receives sensible probability if
it resembles sequences that were. [S-29] Later work found that language
models trained only to predict text began to perform tasks such as
answering questions and translating without explicit supervision for
those tasks, and that this behavior strengthened with scale. [S-44]
[S-26] None of this is stored as a neat entry in a particular parameter
or unit; what the model has is a set of parameters that jointly produce
good predictions, and the question of exactly where a given capability
lives inside them is an open research topic, not something this page can
state.

## 7. The objective is prediction, not verification

Pretraining teaches the model to predict statistical patterns in its
data. Factual accuracy can emerge because factual regularities are
present in that data: if a fact is stated consistently across many
documents, predicting those documents well requires reproducing it. But
independent verification of truth is not itself the pretraining
objective. The loss at a position is lowered by assigning probability to
whatever token actually followed in the training text, whether that text
was accurate or not, and ordinary autoregressive decoding does not itself
include the training loss or an independent truth-verification
objective. [S-08] A surrounding system can separately add retrieval,
verifiers, tools, reranking, or other checks; later pages cover those.

Two conclusions that do not follow should be named. The objective does
not make the model a copy of its training data; it produces a function
that generalizes to sequences it never saw, as §6 describes. And it is
not accurate to say that next-token prediction "causes" false outputs, as
though a different objective would remove them; the precise statement is
that the objective rewards plausible continuation and does not check
truth, so a fluent, unsupported continuation is not penalized as such.
How that plays out in deployed models, and what grounding and external
checks add, is the subject of later pages.

## 8. Pretraining, post-training, and inference-time context

Three different things happen to a model over its life, and only two of
them change its parameters.

**Pretraining** is this page: large-scale training on the next-token
objective, changing every trainable parameter.

**Post-training** also changes parameters, using further training with
different data and objectives. It is a family of methods rather than one
fixed procedure: supervised training on demonstrations of desired
behavior, optimization toward human or model preferences, reinforcement
learning, and safety or behavior shaping are all members of it. A later
lesson covers them; this page only marks that they, too, are parameter
changes.

**Inference-time context** changes no parameter at all. Instructions,
the conversation so far, retrieved documents, tool results, and files or
other state supplied to the current call are tokens in the context
window, as `learn/tokens-context.qmd` describes; they shape this call's
prediction and leave the parameters as they were. [S-31] If a product
keeps a memory, a file, or a project state between sessions, that
persistence is implemented by the surrounding software, which stores the
information and supplies it again later. It is not a parameter update,
and calling it "training" or "learning" in the sense of this page would
be wrong.

## 9. Training and generation are not the same computation

At training time, many target positions of a complete sequence are
evaluated in parallel under the causal mask, a loss is computed from all
of them, backpropagation computes gradients, and the optimizer updates
the parameters. At inference time, the parameters are normally fixed;
the model predicts a distribution for the next token, one token is
selected by argmax or by sampling, and the selected token becomes part
of the context for the prediction after it. [S-07]

One implementation detail is worth a sentence because it is often
described loosely. When generating token by token, the keys and values
computed for earlier positions do not change from one step to the next,
so implementations typically store them and reuse them instead of
recomputing every earlier position's attention inputs at every step; the
cost of repeatedly loading those stored keys and values is a recognized
bottleneck of step-by-step decoding. [S-43] This reuse is an efficiency
measure. The mathematics of autoregression, each token predicted from
the tokens before it, is the same with or without it.

## 10. Check your understanding

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>Why can a transformer compute the training loss for every
position of a sequence in one forward pass, when generation has to
proceed one token at a time?</summary>
Because during training the whole sequence is already known, and causal
masking guarantees that the prediction at each position uses only the
positions before it. All positions can therefore be evaluated together
without any prediction seeing its own target. During generation the
later tokens do not exist until they are selected, so each step must
wait for the previous one (§2, §9).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>A model assigns probability 0.05 to the observed next token at
one position and 0.50 at another. Which position contributes more to the
loss, and by roughly how much?</summary>
The first. Its loss is $-\log 0.05 \approx 3.0$ against $-\log 0.50
\approx 0.69$, so it contributes more than four times as much. Lowering
the loss means raising the probability assigned to observed tokens
(§3, §5).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>What does backpropagation change?</summary>
Nothing. It computes the gradient of the batch loss with respect to every
trainable parameter. The optimizer then uses those gradients to update
the parameters in a separate step (§4).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>Which of these change the model's parameters: pretraining,
post-training, a document placed in the context window, a tool result
returned to the model?</summary>
Pretraining and post-training. A document in the context and a tool
result are inference-time context: they change what the model is
conditioning on for this call and leave the parameters untouched (§8).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>Does the pretraining objective check whether the training text
is true?</summary>
No. It rewards assigning probability to whatever token actually followed.
Factual regularities in the data can make accurate prediction and
accurate statements coincide, but truth verification is not part of the
objective (§7).
</details>
:::

## 11. Continue learning

- **Radford et al., *Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask
  Learners*** (paper, the GPT-2 report; Section 2 states the objective
  in one paragraph). Technical level. Especially good for seeing the
  autoregressive factorization written down for a transformer language
  model, and for the claim that prediction alone led to task behavior.
  Limitation: a 2019 model and dataset; the training details are brief.
  <https://cdn.openai.com/better-language-models/language_models_are_unsupervised_multitask_learners.pdf>

- **Bengio, Ducharme, Vincent, and Jauvin, *A Neural Probabilistic
  Language Model*** (paper, Journal of Machine Learning Research 3,
  2003; Sections 1 and 2). Technical level. The clearest early statement
  that a neural network can be trained by maximizing the log-likelihood
  of next-word predictions and that learned vectors are what make it
  generalize. Limitation: not a transformer, and a word rather than
  subword vocabulary.
  <https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume3/bengio03a/bengio03a.pdf>

- **Andrej Karpathy, *Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT*** (video, 3.5
  hours; the pretraining discussion occupies its first part).
  Introductory level, plain language. Especially good for the scale and
  the practical shape of pretraining on real data. Limitation: no
  equations, and no timestamp is given here because none has been
  verified for this course.
  <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7xTGNNLPyMI>

See `resources.qmd` for the complete list of sources used across this
course, with full source-map entries.
